def: The US electronic network that moves money between bank accounts. Most funding payments are collected by ACH debit on a daily, weekly or monthly schedule.
The yearly cost of borrowing expressed as a percentage, including interest and certain fees. Useful for comparing loans; MCAs are not loans and are usually quoted with a factor rate instead.
The lump sum you receive from a merchant cash advance before any fees are deducted.
Paying off a loan through scheduled payments that cover both interest and principal, so the balance reaches zero at the end of the term.
The average amount in your business bank account each day over a statement period. Underwriters use it to gauge cushion and payment capacity.
Approving funding mainly from recent business bank statements — deposits, balances and activity — rather than tax returns or financial statements.
A company that connects businesses with funding partners and helps compare offers, rather than lending its own money. Fidelity Funding is a broker.
A revolving credit limit you can draw from as needed, paying interest only on what you use and regaining access as you repay.
How long cash is tied up between paying for inventory or labor and collecting from customers: days inventory + days receivable − days payable.
A card transaction reversed by the customer's bank after a dispute. Frequent chargebacks raise processing costs and can concern underwriters.
An asset pledged to secure financing, which the funder can claim if you don't repay — for example, the equipment in an equipment loan.
A contract clause in which a borrower agrees in advance to a court judgment if they default. Its enforceability varies by state; read contracts carefully and consult an attorney.
Combining several advances or loans into one, usually to reduce the number or size of payments. It can lower or raise total cost depending on terms.
The total dollar cost of funding: what you repay minus what you actually receive.
How much of your available credit you're using. Lower utilization generally helps credit scores.
Cash available for debt payments divided by required debt payments. A DSCR above 1.0 means income covers payments.
The IRS tax ID for a business, used on funding applications in place of an owner's SSN for the business itself.
A reduction in the remaining balance offered by some MCA funders if you repay early. Not every contract includes one — ask before signing.
Total card-processing fees divided by total card volume for a period — the clearest measure of what accepting cards costs you.
Financing for vehicles, machinery or technology where the equipment typically serves as collateral.
A multiplier used to price merchant cash advances. Advance × factor rate = total payback; a $50,000 advance at 1.30 repays $65,000.
Selling unpaid customer invoices to a factoring company for an immediate advance, minus a fee.
A credit inquiry that can affect your credit score, usually performed when you move forward with a specific funder.
The percentage of daily card sales withheld to repay a merchant cash advance in split-funding arrangements.
The fee card-issuing banks charge on each card transaction — the largest part of processing costs, set by the card networks.
A processing pricing model that passes interchange through at cost and adds a disclosed markup, making true costs easier to see.
A purchase of a portion of your future sales for an upfront lump sum, repaid through a share of receipts or fixed ACH debits.
The monthly report from your card processor showing volume, transactions and every fee charged.
A payment returned because the account didn't have enough money. Frequent NSFs can weaken a funding application.
Days your business bank account balance falls below zero. Underwriters watch them closely.
The amount that actually reaches your account after origination or other upfront fees are subtracted.
An upfront fee charged for setting up financing, often deducted from the amount funded.
The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard — security requirements for any business that accepts card payments.
A promise by a business owner to be personally responsible for repaying business funding if the business can't.
An MCA's place in line when a business has more than one advance — first position, second position, and so on.
A fee some loans charge if you repay early. Ask whether one applies before you sign.
Funding that pays your supplier so you can fulfill a confirmed customer order.
A contract provision allowing MCA payments to be adjusted to reflect actual sales if revenue drops.
Additional funding offered after you've repaid a meaningful share of an existing advance or loan.
Funding repaid as a share of future revenue, so payments rise and fall with sales.
A loan made by a lender and partially guaranteed by the US Small Business Administration, such as the 7(a) and 504 programs. Often low-cost but slower to close.
A credit check that doesn't affect your credit score. Fidelity's initial review uses a soft pull.
Taking a new merchant cash advance while existing ones are still being repaid, which can quickly strain cash flow.
Adding a fee to card transactions to offset processing costs. Rules vary by state and card network.
The length of time over which funding is repaid.
How long your business has been operating — a key underwriting factor.
The full amount you'll repay over the life of the funding, including all costs.
A public notice filed by a funder claiming a security interest in business assets.
The funder's review of your business's revenue, history and risk to decide whether to fund and on what terms.
Financing without specific collateral, often backed by a personal guarantee instead.
Current assets minus current liabilities — the cash available to run day-to-day operations.
